us.title: Two Killed, Officers Hurt in Downtown Minneapolis Shooting
us.metaDescription: A shooting at a downtown Minneapolis apartment building left two people dead and multiple officers injured Wednesday as police and the FBI responded.
us.excerpt: A shooting inside a downtown Minneapolis apartment building left two people dead and several others wounded, including police officers, prompting a large emergency response and warnings for residents to avoid the Loring Park area.
us.imageAlt: Police vehicles and law enforcement officers gathered outside an apartment building in downtown Minneapolis after a shooting
keyTakeaways: Two people were killed and multiple others wounded, including three Minneapolis police officers, after a shooting at a downtown apartment building near Loring Park on Wednesday afternoon.
The suspected gunman was found dead at the scene; police have not released his identity and said the cause of his death remains unclear.
Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz, Minneapolis Mayor Jacob Frey and FBI Director Kash Patel confirmed state and federal resources were supporting the local investigation.

content.text: A shooting inside a downtown Minneapolis apartment building left two people dead and several others wounded Wednesday afternoon, including three police officers, in an incident that prompted a massive law enforcement response and warnings for residents to avoid the area around Loring Park.

The suspected gunman was also found dead at the scene, according to Minneapolis police. Officials said Wednesday evening that they had not yet determined how he died and had not released his identity.
Timeline of the Shooting and Police Response

Minneapolis police said a 911 call reporting shots fired came in shortly after 4:30 p.m. at an apartment building in the 15 East Grant Street area, within the Loring Park neighborhood near the Minneapolis Convention Center. Officers arrived within roughly two to three minutes and entered the building, where they found multiple victims in the lobby, according to Interim Police Chief Bill Peterson.

As officers moved through the building, they heard additional gunfire and followed the sound to an upper floor, Peterson said. There, responding officers encountered what he described as a haze that significantly limited visibility, though he did not provide further detail on its source. City officials later said several additional officers experienced adverse effects after exposure to an unknown airborne substance at the scene.
The building has been identified by city officials as Shoreline Plaza, a high-rise formerly known as Loring Towers.
Officers Among the Wounded

Police Sgt. Garrett Parten said at an evening news conference that three Minneapolis police officers were injured during the response. Two were shot, one in the leg and another twice in the abdomen, while a third officer sustained injuries not caused by gunfire. Hennepin County Medical Center said all three officers were in stable condition and expected to make a full recovery. City officials said two additional officers were separately injured when a squad car responding to the scene was involved in a crash.

Peterson said one of the two civilian victims was fatally shot at the scene, while the second died after being taken to Hennepin County Medical Center. The hospital said it received seven patients in total but did not release additional details about their conditions. Authorities said three other civilians were shot and were being treated at the hospital.

"This is a tremendously tragic event, and our thoughts and prayers are with the families, the loved ones of those who lost their lives, those who were injured and with the injured officers and their families," Parten said.

Peterson added that he was sickened by the level of violence, but said that feeling was tempered by the actions of responding officers, who he said confronted an extraordinarily dangerous situation without hesitation.
What Authorities Have Said About the Suspect

Police have not released the name of the suspected shooter and said they were not doing so at this stage of the investigation. Officials said the individual was known to police prior to the shooting but declined to discuss a possible motive. Parten said it remained unclear exactly how the suspect died.
Community Impact and Area Response

The shooting unfolded during the evening rush hour, snarling traffic in the surrounding downtown area, which is home to the Minneapolis Convention Center, several hotels, a hospital and Loring Park itself. The nearby University of St. Thomas Minneapolis campus issued a shelter-in-place order for students and staff out of caution while the situation was active.

Video shared on social media showed officers with rifles raised toward the upper floors of the apartment tower as law enforcement vehicles with lights and sirens converged on the block. City officials urged the public to steer clear of the broader Loring Park area while the response was underway.

Law enforcement agencies from across the region assisted Minneapolis police at the scene, including the Minnesota State Patrol, the Hennepin County Sheriff's Office, the Minneapolis Park Police, the St. Paul Police Department, the University of Minnesota Police Department, and police departments from several neighboring suburbs.
Statements From State and Federal Officials

Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz said in a social media post that state officials were on the ground assisting local law enforcement. "Grateful to law enforcement actively working to ensure the safety of our neighbors in Downtown Minneapolis this afternoon," Walz wrote. "Minnesota is praying for our first responders."

Minneapolis Mayor Jacob Frey said neighboring police agencies and the Minnesota State Patrol were working closely with the Minneapolis Police Department in response to the shooting. Minnesota House Speaker Lisa Demuth said she was praying for the victims of what she called a heinous crime.

FBI Director Kash Patel said the bureau was responding to the shooting and would offer all resources necessary to assist local authorities. The FBI assisted personnel at the scene alongside local and state law enforcement throughout the evening.
What Investigators Are Looking Into Next

Minneapolis police have not yet disclosed a motive for the shooting or confirmed additional details about how the confrontation unfolded once officers reached the upper floor of the building. Investigators are also still working to determine the exact circumstances surrounding the suspected shooter's death, along with the source of the haze that officers encountered during their response.

Authorities have not indicated whether any additional individuals are being sought in connection with the shooting. Officials said the investigation remains active and that further updates would be provided as confirmed information becomes available.

us.metaTitle: Edouard Floods East Texas, Prompts Rescues
us.title: Tropical Storm Edouard Floods East Texas, Triggers Rescues
us.metaDescription: Former Tropical Storm Edouard dumped up to 20 inches of rain on East Texas, flooding homes and roads and prompting dozens of emergency rescues.
us.excerpt: Former Tropical Storm Edouard stalled over rural East Texas, dumping nearly two feet of rain, flooding roads and homes, and triggering dozens of emergency rescues as three hurricanes churned simultaneously in the Pacific Ocean.
us.imageAlt: Flooded roadway in East Texas after heavy rainfall from former Tropical Storm Edouard
keyTakeaways: Former Tropical Storm Edouard dumped up to 20 inches of rain on Hardin, Tyler and Polk counties in East Texas, triggering flash flood emergencies and disaster declarations.
Emergency crews rescued 12 motorists from flooded roads, two residents from a flooded home, and 21 people from a damaged assisted living facility in Hardin County.
About 77,000 Texas utility customers lost power as the storm's 90 mph wind gusts downed trees and lines, even as the system weakened into a tropical depression expected to dissipate by Thursday.

content.text: Rescue crews across East Texas pulled dozens of people from flooded cars, homes and an assisted living facility this week after former Tropical Storm Edouard stalled over the region and unleashed nearly two feet of rain in some communities. The storm, which made landfall Tuesday before weakening into a tropical depression, continued dumping heavy rain into Wednesday, prompting flash flood emergencies in several counties near the Louisiana border.

The National Weather Service said the heaviest rainfall was expected to keep threatening the eastern part of the state through Thursday morning before the system finally dissipates. At the same time, forecasters were tracking an unusually active stretch of tropical weather in the Pacific Ocean, where three separate hurricanes were spinning simultaneously in open waters.
Extreme Rainfall Totals Across East Texas

Edouard's slow track inland concentrated its heaviest rain over a cluster of counties northeast of Houston, particularly Hardin, Tyler and Polk counties. The National Weather Service reported that areas between the towns of Kountze and Warren received upward of 20 inches of rain, with additional accumulations of one to five inches possible before the system moves out. In Hardin County alone, totals ranged between 18 and 20 inches over a two-day span, according to the weather service.

Nick Slaughter, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service, noted that Hardin County typically sees an average of just 5.51 inches of rain for the entire month of September, underscoring how far Edouard's rainfall totals exceeded normal conditions for the area. Flash flood emergencies, the most serious level of flood alert issued by the weather service, were declared for portions of both Hardin and Tyler counties as floodwaters rose rapidly.
Texas Flooding and Emergency Response

Officials in Hardin and Polk counties formally declared disasters in response to the flooding, and dozens of school districts across the affected region canceled classes Wednesday as rising water made many roads impassable. In areas closest to the Louisiana border, municipal offices also closed and residents were urged to stay off the roads and remain home.

Hardin County's office of emergency management said Wednesday afternoon that crews had rescued 12 motorists who drove into flooded roadways, along with two residents pulled from a flooded home. Roughly 10 structures in the county sustained damage from falling trees, and thousands of residents remained without power as cleanup efforts continued.

An assisted living facility in Hardin County was also damaged by the flooding, forcing the evacuation of 21 residents. Texas Parks and Wildlife said its game wardens assisted with the evacuation, and photos released by the agency showed officials wading through thigh-deep water in parts of the county during rescue operations.
Damage to Homes, Roads and Power Infrastructure

Beyond the flooding itself, Edouard's winds caused significant damage as it came ashore Tuesday. The storm produced wind gusts as high as 90 mph, with sustained gusts of about 70 mph reported near Port Arthur and 67 mph near Beaumont as the system moved through the coastal region. Storm-chaser footage captured a collapsed wall at Sabine Pass Independent School, and downed power lines sparked at least one small fire in Nederland after igniting nearby vegetation.

In neighboring Jefferson County, the primary concern shifted to restoring electricity after trees and limbs toppled onto power lines throughout the storm. Robert Grimm, the county's emergency management coordinator, said about 22,000 customers in Jefferson County remained without power late Wednesday afternoon, accounting for nearly half of the roughly 50,000 utility customers affected statewide at that point. By Wednesday evening, statewide outage tracking site poweroutage.com reported the total climbing to approximately 77,000 customers, with Jefferson, Hardin and Polk counties reporting the highest concentrations.

Grady Leger, a resident near Lumberton in Hardin County, described the moment a power line came down near his home Tuesday evening. "Some blue and yellow, white sparks caught part of my dead tree on fire," Leger said, adding that he could feel vibrations coming up through the ground as the line fell.

Roadways across the region also sustained damage or remained impassable well into Wednesday. Texas transportation officials reported flooding on Highway 69 North in Kountze and on FM Road 1013 near Hillister, while rising water was also observed on creeks in Silsbee, Sour Lake and Bevil Oaks.
Three Hurricanes Active in the Pacific Ocean

While Edouard soaked East Texas, the National Hurricane Center in Miami was tracking a separate burst of activity across the Pacific. Hurricane Marie strengthened from a tropical storm on Wednesday well offshore of southwestern Mexico, with forecasters warning that swells generated by the storm were expected to affect coastal southwestern Mexico and Mexico's Baja California peninsula over the following days, before likely spreading toward Southern California by the weekend.

Hurricane Lowell, a powerful Category 4 storm several hundred miles south of Hawaii, briefly intensified to Category 5 strength before weakening slightly, though forecasters said it was expected to remain a powerful system in the days ahead. Swells generated by Lowell were already beginning to affect portions of the Hawaiian islands. The hurricane center warned that swells from both Marie and Lowell were likely to produce life-threatening surf and rip current conditions along affected coastlines.

A third system, Hurricane Karina, also strengthened into a powerful Category 4 hurricane elsewhere in the Pacific, though forecasters expect it to weaken gradually over the coming days. None of the three Pacific storms posed a direct threat to the US mainland as of Wednesday.
Forecast and What Comes Next for Texas

Forecasters expect Edouard's remnants to finally dissipate over eastern Texas by Thursday morning, though leftover moisture from the system could still fuel scattered showers and thunderstorms across the region into Thursday. The overall flood threat is expected to ease as the system weakens further, though standing water and saturated ground will likely keep some roads hazardous even after the rain stops.

Edouard's brief but intense run through Texas fits a broader pattern for the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season, which has produced relatively short-lived systems and has been running well below its historical average pace of activity so far this year.
Ongoing Recovery and Safety Guidance for Residents

Emergency management officials in Hardin County said response and recovery work would continue in the days ahead as floodwaters slowly recede from roads and neighborhoods. Downed trees, tangled power lines and scattered debris remain hazards in several communities, and some roadways are still difficult or impossible to navigate safely.

Officials continued urging residents to stay off flooded roadways, avoid downed power lines and give utility and emergency crews room to complete repair and cleanup work. Utility providers, including Entergy, have been working to restore service to tens of thousands of customers across the affected counties, though full restoration is expected to take additional time given the scale of the damage to the region's power infrastructure.

us.metaTitle: Clancy Jury Deadlocked, Mistrial Risk Grows
us.title: Lindsay Clancy Jury Remains Deadlocked as Mistrial Looms
us.metaDescription: The jury in Lindsay Clancy's murder trial remains deadlocked after days of deliberation, raising the risk of a mistrial in the Massachusetts case.
us.excerpt: Jurors in the murder trial of Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts mother accused of killing her three children, have twice told the court they cannot reach a unanimous verdict, pushing the closely watched case toward a possible mistrial.
us.imageAlt: Plymouth Superior Court in Massachusetts where the Lindsay Clancy murder trial jury has deliberated for multiple days
keyTakeaways: The 12-person jury in Lindsay Clancy's murder trial has twice told Judge William Sullivan it is deadlocked, and he has now issued a special 'dynamite charge' urging jurors to keep working toward a verdict.

Clancy does not dispute strangling her three children in 2023; her defense argues postpartum psychosis left her not criminally responsible, while prosecutors say she acted intentionally and rationally.
If jurors remain unable to agree, Judge Sullivan could declare a mistrial, after which prosecutors would decide whether to retry Clancy, seek a plea deal, or drop the charges.

content.text: The jury weighing murder charges against Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts mother accused of killing her three young children in 2023, remains deadlocked after multiple days of deliberation, raising a growing risk that the closely watched trial could end without a verdict. Jurors have twice told the court they cannot reach a unanimous decision, prompting Judge William Sullivan to issue a special instruction urging them to keep trying before he considers declaring a mistrial.

Clancy, 36, a former labor and delivery nurse, does not dispute that she strangled her children, Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months, with exercise resistance bands inside the family's Duxbury home in January 2023. The central legal question facing jurors is not whether she caused her children's deaths, but whether she was criminally responsible for her actions at the time, a distinction that has placed postpartum psychosis and the legal standard for criminal responsibility at the heart of the case.
A Deadlocked Jury and the Judge's Response

The 12-person jury, made up of nine women and three men, began deliberating in late August after roughly a month of testimony. By early September, after nearly 30 hours of deliberation spread across multiple days, jurors sent Judge Sullivan a note stating they were unable to reach a unanimous decision. Sullivan initially responded by directing them to continue deliberating, but when jurors reported the same impasse a second time, he read them what is formally known as the Tuey-Rodriguez instruction, sometimes referred to informally as a "dynamite charge."

That instruction asks jurors to reconsider the reasonableness of their own views and those of fellow jurors without abandoning their sincerely held convictions simply to reach agreement. Sullivan told jurors that no one could say a future jury would be more intelligent, impartial or capable of deciding the case than the one currently seated. Massachusetts courts generally treat the Tuey-Rodriguez charge as a final, formal push toward a verdict, and if jurors continue to report deadlock after receiving it, a judge may move to declare a mistrial.
The Evidence and Testimony Presented at Trial

Over the course of the trial, prosecutors called more than 70 witnesses, including members of Clancy's family, friends, first responders, investigators and medical providers, before resting their case in mid-August. The defense subsequently called ten witnesses of its own, including psychiatric experts who testified that Clancy was suffering from postpartum psychosis at the time of the killings. Prosecutors later presented a rebuttal case featuring three additional mental health experts who testified that Clancy was not psychotic when she killed her children.

Jurors also heard testimony describing the decline in Clancy's mental health in the months leading up to the killings, including details about medications she had been prescribed and a brief stay at a psychiatric hospital. The trial included roughly 300 exhibits for jurors to review, a volume defense attorney Kevin Reddington said outside the courthouse has required considerable effort from the panel. "They've been incredibly hard-working, paying attention through the whole trial," Reddington told reporters.
The Role of Postpartum Psychosis in the Defense

Clancy's defense has centered on the argument that she should not be held criminally responsible because she was in the grip of severe postpartum psychosis when she killed her children. Her attorneys have said she believed she heard a voice instructing her to kill the children so that she could then end her own life. After the killings, Clancy jumped from a second-floor window of the home in an apparent suicide attempt and remains paralyzed from the waist down.

Prosecutors have pushed back on that account, arguing that Clancy acted "intentionally, rationally and swiftly," and have questioned the seriousness of her suicide attempt. They have also argued that Clancy deliberately sent her then-husband, Patrick Clancy, out of the home on errands before carrying out the killings, which prosecutors say points to premeditation rather than a psychotic break.

Patrick Clancy testified as the trial's first witness after opening statements in late July. He has said in public interviews that he forgives his now ex-wife, describing her as someone who was ill rather than someone who acted out of malice.
What Happens if Jurors Cannot Reach a Verdict

If the jury remains unable to agree even after the Tuey-Rodriguez instruction, Judge Sullivan has the authority to declare a mistrial due to a hung jury. A mistrial would not resolve the underlying charges against Clancy, which would remain pending. Prosecutors would then need to decide whether to retry the case before an entirely new jury, attempt to negotiate a plea agreement with Clancy's defense team, or drop the charges altogether.

Legal analysts not involved in the case have noted that Massachusetts has seen deadlocked juries lead to mistrials in other high-profile cases in recent years, including the first murder trial of Karen Read in 2024, which ended in a hung jury before prosecutors retried the case; Read was ultimately acquitted following a 2025 retrial. Brad Bailey, a Boston defense attorney and former prosecutor who is not involved in the Clancy case, has said that while a retrial remains possible, Clancy's defense team is likely to push prosecutors toward dropping the charges rather than proceeding through another full trial.
Possible Verdicts if Jurors Reach a Decision

Should the jury ultimately reach a unanimous decision, several outcomes remain legally possible. Jurors could convict Clancy of first-degree murder, second-degree murder or manslaughter if they conclude she was criminally responsible for her children's deaths, with a murder conviction carrying the possibility of a life prison sentence. Alternatively, jurors could acquit Clancy if they find her mental state at the time meets the legal standard for lacking criminal responsibility. Even in the event of an acquittal, a judge could still order Clancy confined to a mental health facility if a subsequent evaluation determines she poses a danger to the public.
A Case That Has Drawn National Attention

The trial, which has been livestreamed and drawn packed courtrooms of reporters and spectators since jury selection began in July, has stirred broader public debate over maternal mental health after childbirth and how the criminal justice system should weigh severe postpartum psychiatric illness against personal culpability. The case has divided public opinion, with some viewing Clancy as a mother failed by inadequate mental health treatment and others focused on the loss of three young lives.
What Comes Next in the Court Process

For now, deliberations are set to continue, with jurors returning to the Plymouth Superior Court courtroom to resume their discussions. Judge Sullivan has thanked jurors repeatedly for their diligence and instructed them not to discuss, read about or research the case outside the courtroom. Whether the panel ultimately reaches a unanimous verdict or the judge is forced to declare a mistrial, the case is expected to remain a focal point of both legal and public attention given the questions it raises about mental illness, motherhood and criminal accountability under Massachusetts law.

us.metaTitle: Judge Blocks Trump's New Birthright Citizenship Order
us.title: Federal Judge Blocks Trump's Latest Birthright Citizenship Order
us.metaDescription: A federal judge blocked Trump's new executive order limiting birthright citizenship, citing Supreme Court precedent and the 14th Amendment.
us.excerpt: A federal judge in Maryland has blocked President Trump's newest attempt to narrow birthright citizenship, ruling the executive order is likely unconstitutional and citing a Supreme Court decision that struck down a similar effort earlier this year.
us.imageAlt: The United States Constitution with a gavel, representing a federal court ruling on birthright citizenship under the 14th Amendment
keyTakeaways: US District Judge Deborah Boardman issued a preliminary injunction blocking Trump's August 2026 executive order narrowing birthright citizenship, calling it 'almost certainly unconstitutional.'
The ruling cites the Supreme Court's June decision that struck down Trump's original 2025 birthright citizenship order, which sought to deny citizenship based on parents' immigration status.
The administration is expected to appeal the injunction, potentially setting up another Supreme Court review of the scope of the 14th Amendment's Citizenship Clause.

content.text: A federal judge in Maryland has blocked President Donald Trump's latest attempt to narrow birthright citizenship, ruling that his newest executive order is likely unconstitutional and directly conflicts with a Supreme Court decision issued just months earlier. US District Judge Deborah Boardman issued a preliminary injunction Wednesday against the order, which the administration had framed as an effort to curb so-called birth tourism and close what officials described as loopholes in citizenship law.

The ruling marks the second time in 2026 that a court has stopped Trump from implementing changes to birthright citizenship, a right guaranteed under the 14th Amendment since its ratification in 1868. It also intensifies a legal standoff between the White House and federal courts that has already reached the Supreme Court once this year and appears likely to return there.
What the Judge Ruled

In a 35-page opinion, Boardman wrote that Trump's August executive order limiting who qualifies for automatic citizenship at birth "is almost certainly unconstitutional," and granted a preliminary injunction preventing federal agencies from enforcing it while the underlying lawsuit proceeds. The injunction applies to a certified class of plaintiffs represented in the case and blocks the government from denying citizenship documents to children who fall within the categories targeted by the order.

"The Supreme Court has spoken: Children in the certified class are 'citizens at birth,'" Boardman wrote, directly invoking the high court's June ruling that struck down an earlier, broader version of Trump's birthright citizenship order. She added that the president has, since the start of his second term in January 2025, repeatedly used executive action to try to "upend our country's longstanding tradition of birthright citizenship" and narrow rights guaranteed under the Citizenship Clause.

Boardman, who was appointed to the federal bench by President Joe Biden, is not new to this litigation. She previously blocked an earlier version of Trump's birthright citizenship order in February 2025, issuing a nationwide injunction at that time after finding that no court in the country had ever endorsed the administration's interpretation of the 14th Amendment. In this latest ruling, she reiterated that position, writing that no court has sided with the administration's reading of the Constitution on this issue and that her court "will not be the first."
The Constitutional Foundation of Birthright Citizenship

Birthright citizenship traces back to the Citizenship Clause of the 14th Amendment, ratified in 1868 in the aftermath of the Civil War. Under longstanding legal interpretation, the amendment guarantees that virtually anyone born on US soil is automatically a citizen at birth, regardless of their parents' immigration status, with only narrow, historically recognized exceptions such as children born to foreign diplomats. That interpretation has governed US citizenship law and practice for more than 150 years.
What the August Executive Order Sought to Do

Trump's August order was a narrower follow-up to a more sweeping directive he signed on his first day back in office in January 2025, which had sought to deny citizenship to children born to parents who were in the country illegally or on a temporary basis. The Supreme Court struck down that original order in June, prompting the administration to draft a revised version targeting more specific categories of people.

The August order sought to deny automatic citizenship to children born to parents connected to foreign embassies or organizations, to anyone the administration classified as an "alien enemy," and to those the order described as engaging in "birth tourism," defined as entering the US on a nonimmigrant visa specifically to give birth on American soil. The order also targeted children born to adults who the government determined had "engaged in a commercial transaction to purchase or access birthright citizenship," a category that left some families concerned that ordinary actions, such as purchasing airfare to the US before becoming pregnant, could be used against them.
Arguments From the Families and Advocacy Groups

The lawsuit was brought by a group of immigrant families along with three advocacy organizations: We Are CASA, the Asylum Seeker Advocacy Project, and the Institute for Constitutional Advocacy and Protection. The plaintiffs argued that the executive branch had applied an overly broad and inconsistent standard for determining who counts as an "alien enemy," at times relying on speculation or unverified information rather than clear evidence.

Some families told the court they feared their children could lose access to citizenship simply because a distant relative had a tangential connection to a gang in their home country, even though the parents themselves had no such ties. Attorneys for the plaintiffs said the resulting uncertainty left affected families in a state of confusion and fear about their children's legal status.

Shana Khader, legal director at We Are CASA, said in a statement following the ruling that the administration would not succeed in its efforts. "The White House must recognize it will not succeed in stripping children of their right to citizenship, evading binding court decisions or placing the president's anti-immigrant agenda above the Constitution," Khader said.
The Administration's Position

Government attorneys had argued that the request to block the order was premature, contending that the federal agencies responsible for enforcing it would rely on "appropriate measures" and official guidance that had not yet been issued. Boardman rejected that argument directly, writing that regardless of what future guidance might say, the order itself "commands agencies to deny citizenship documents to several broad categories of children," meaning the harm to affected families was not speculative.

The judge also wrote separately that the government could not claim a legitimate interest in enforcing an order she considers likely unconstitutional, and that the narrow carve-outs described in the August order bear little resemblance to the limited historical exceptions to birthright citizenship that the Supreme Court has previously recognized. The White House did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the ruling.
Previous Legal Battles Over Birthright Citizenship

This is not the first time federal courts have intervened to stop changes to birthright citizenship under the current administration. Trump's original January 2025 order was blocked by multiple federal judges within weeks of its signing, including a ruling from Seattle-based Judge John Coughenour, who at the time described the order as "blatantly unconstitutional" and said in more than four decades on the bench he could not recall a case so clearly at odds with the Constitution. Boardman's own nationwide injunction against that earlier order followed shortly after, setting the stage for the case's eventual path to the Supreme Court, which ruled against the administration in June.
What Happens Next in the Legal Process

Wednesday's ruling is a preliminary injunction, meaning it blocks enforcement of the August order while the underlying class-action lawsuit continues, rather than issuing a final, permanent resolution of the case. The administration is widely expected to appeal the decision, a move that could send the dispute to the US Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit and, potentially, back to the Supreme Court for further review of how far a president's executive authority extends over the scope of the Citizenship Clause.
Broader Implications for Immigration Law and Presidential Authority

The repeated legal setbacks underscore a broader constitutional question that has repeatedly resurfaced throughout Trump's second term: whether a president can use executive orders to reshape citizenship rules that have traditionally been understood as fixed by constitutional text and longstanding Supreme Court precedent. Wednesday's decision suggests that, for now, federal courts continue to view birthright citizenship as settled constitutional law rather than a policy question open to reinterpretation through executive action, even as the administration continues to test that boundary through successive, narrower versions of its original order.

us.metaTitle: Whistleblower warns USPS mail-ballot system could disrupt the midterms
us.title: Whistleblower warns USPS mail-ballot system could disrupt the midterms
us.metaDescription: A federal official's disclosure alleges the Postal Service's rushed new ballot-verification system could prevent millions of Americans from receiving their mail ballots on time.
us.excerpt: A federal official's disclosure alleges the Postal Service's rushed new ballot-verification system could prevent millions of Americans from receiving their mail ballots on time.
us.imageAlt: Mail ballots being sorted, illustrating concerns over the USPS mail-voting system
keyTakeaways: A whistleblower says the new USPS ballot portal is untested and rushed
A single failed barcode scan could reject an entire batch of 10,000 ballots
Key parts of the underlying executive order remain blocked in federal court

content.text: A federal whistleblower has warned that a new Postal Service system for processing mail ballots is so rushed and untested that it risks disrupting the upcoming midterm elections, according to a disclosure made public this week. The anonymous official, whose account was provided to Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut through the nonprofit group Whistleblower Aid, raised what the disclosure describes as grave concerns that the Trump administration has downplayed the likelihood of major failures in ballot delivery.

At the center of the complaint is a new Postal Service IT system, described internally as a portal, that is meant to verify mail ballots against a federal database before they reach voters. According to the whistleblower, the system's design creates an unusually high risk of mass failure: if even a single barcode among a batch of 10,000 ballots fails to scan correctly during verification, the entire batch could be rejected and sent back to the state that issued it, potentially stranding thousands of voters without ballots just as the midterm voting window opens.
A system built under legal pressure

The portal stems from an executive order signed by President Trump earlier this year directing federal agencies to tighten verification requirements for mail-in voting, part of a broader push the administration has framed as an effort to curb illegal voting by non-citizens, even though independent studies and audits have repeatedly found such cases to be extremely rare. A federal judge has already blocked key parts of the order from taking effect while litigation over its constitutionality continues, but the whistleblower alleges the Postal Service has continued quietly building out the system anyway, potentially in violation of that court order.

Blumenthal, who has emerged as one of the sharpest critics of the plan, said the disclosure shows the agency has effectively designed a system that is likely to fail Americans rather than protect the integrity of their votes. He described the technical shortcuts alleged in the whistleblower's account as "mind-boggling" and said he found it difficult to view the rushed rollout, timed for a September 1 implementation target, as anything other than reckless given how directly it could affect voters' ability to cast a ballot in a race already expected to be closely contested nationwide.
The White House pushes back

A Postal Service spokesperson defended the new system, describing it as part of a broader, year-round effort to ensure election mail is handled securely and efficiently, and characterizing the portal as a simple tool to help state election officials share information about voters receiving mail ballots. The White House has also disputed the whistleblower's characterization of the rollout, though officials have not offered a detailed technical rebuttal of the specific failure scenario described in the disclosure.

With mail voting for the midterms already beginning in several states, the dispute is likely to intensify quickly rather than play out over a leisurely legislative timeline. Voting rights advocates say the coming weeks will be a crucial test of whether the courts can act fast enough to prevent any large-scale disruption before ballots are due, while lawmakers on the relevant committees have indicated they plan further oversight hearings to press Postal Service leadership on exactly how extensively the disputed system has already been deployed despite the ongoing legal challenge.

Election officials in several states have said they are closely monitoring the situation and preparing contingency plans in case the disputed system is allowed to proceed despite the ongoing legal challenge. Voting rights organizations have urged voters who plan to cast ballots by mail to request them as early as possible and to track their status closely, given the uncertainty surrounding how smoothly the new verification process might ultimately function once it is put into practice.

finance.metaTitle: Fed rate-hike odds jump under Chair Warsh as oil shock stokes inflation fears
finance.title: Fed rate-hike odds jump under Chair Warsh as oil shock stokes inflation fears
finance.metaDescription: Traders now see a much higher chance of a Federal Reserve rate increase this month after oil prices surged, reversing expectations that had leaned toward a hold just a week earlier.
finance.excerpt: Traders now see a much higher chance of a Federal Reserve rate increase this month after oil prices surged, reversing expectations that had leaned toward a hold just a week earlier.
finance.imageAlt: Federal Reserve building representing shifting expectations for an interest rate hike
keyTakeaways: Markets now price a roughly 66% chance of a Fed rate hike this month
That figure has flipped from a majority expecting a hold just a week earlier
Fed Chair Kevin Warsh has described the economy as solid despite the pressure

content.text: Expectations for the Federal Reserve's next move have shifted dramatically over the past week, with traders now pricing in a roughly two-thirds chance that the central bank will raise interest rates later this month, a sharp reversal from just days earlier when the majority of market participants expected policymakers to hold steady. The shift comes as oil prices have surged amid renewed conflict between the United States and Iran, reviving inflation concerns that had appeared to be easing over the summer.

According to data tracked by the CME Group's widely followed FedWatch tool, the probability of a quarter-point rate increase this month climbed to roughly 66%, up from about 40% just a week prior. That kind of rapid swing underscores how sensitive monetary policy expectations have become to developments in the Middle East, where the latest round of fighting near the Strait of Hormuz has pushed crude prices to their highest level in more than a month.
Warsh weighs growth against inflation risk

Fed Chair Kevin Warsh has characterized the underlying US economy as solid, pointing to robust business investment, steady consumer spending and labor market conditions broadly consistent with full employment during recent public remarks. That relatively upbeat assessment stands in contrast to concerns raised by some economists earlier this summer, when a disappointing jobs report and downward revisions to prior months' hiring figures had briefly stoked fears that the labor market was weakening more sharply than previously understood.

The renewed spike in energy prices complicates that picture considerably. Inflation remains elevated relative to the Fed's 2% target, a gap the central bank has partly attributed to supply shocks affecting specific sectors, including energy. With oil now trading well above $90 a barrel amid the ongoing conflict, policymakers face a genuinely difficult balancing act between supporting a labor market that has shown signs of softening and containing price pressures that could become more entrenched the longer elevated energy costs persist.
Markets brace for a consequential decision

The stakes of the upcoming decision extend well beyond the immediate rate move itself. Global government bond yields have already climbed to multi-year highs in anticipation of tighter policy, with the 10-year Treasury yield hovering around 4.78% and longer-dated yields pushing back toward levels last seen more than a decade ago. Higher borrowing costs of that magnitude ripple through mortgage rates, corporate financing costs and equity valuations, making the Fed's next move one of the more closely watched events on the calendar for both Wall Street and Main Street alike.

Economists remain divided on which way the Fed will ultimately lean. Some argue that a still-resilient labor market and the risk of inflation expectations becoming unanchored justify moving forward with a hike despite the recent softness in hiring data. Others caution that raising rates into an energy-driven price shock, rather than one rooted in broader demand pressures, risks unnecessarily choking off growth just as consumers are already contending with higher gasoline and heating costs. With the decision still weeks away, traders say the coming data releases, including fresh inflation and employment figures, are likely to keep shifting the odds right up until the Fed's announcement.

Regional Fed officials have offered somewhat differing public assessments of the appropriate path forward, reflecting the genuine uncertainty within the institution itself about how to weigh the competing risks. Some have emphasized the importance of not overreacting to what could prove to be a temporary, geopolitically driven spike in prices, while others have argued that allowing inflation expectations to drift higher, even temporarily, could prove more costly to unwind later than the short-term pain of tighter policy now.

Financial commentators have also noted the unusual optics of a central bank potentially raising rates even as some labor market indicators point toward softness, a combination that has historically been relatively rare and that adds an additional layer of scrutiny to whatever decision the Fed ultimately reaches at its upcoming meeting.

finance.metaTitle: Nvidia Q2 Earnings Crush Estimates on AI Chip Demand
finance.title: Nvidia's AI Chip Demand Drives Q2 Earnings Past Estimates
finance.metaDescription: Nvidia posted $96.22 billion in Q2 revenue and $59.69 billion in net income, beating Wall Street estimates as AI chip and data center demand surged.
finance.excerpt: Nvidia's latest quarterly results topped Wall Street's expectations by a wide margin, with data center revenue more than doubling as hyperscalers continue pouring capital into AI infrastructure despite growing questions about the pace of spending.
finance.imageAlt: Nvidia AI data center GPU chips powering artificial intelligence infrastructure for hyperscale cloud providers
keyTakeaways: Nvidia reported fiscal Q2 net income of $59.69 billion and revenue of $96.22 billion, both far exceeding Wall Street estimates, as data center revenue more than doubled to $89 billion.
CEO Jensen Huang said the company's supply chain is meeting only about 70% of demand, even as Nvidia forecasts $108 billion in revenue for the current quarter and 70% revenue growth for fiscal 2028.

Despite the strong results, Nvidia shares fell 1.6% during the regular session before rising 4.1% after hours, reflecting ongoing investor debate over how long the AI infrastructure spending boom can continue.

content.text: Nvidia once again delivered quarterly results that outpaced Wall Street's expectations, reporting fiscal second-quarter revenue of $96.22 billion and net income of $59.69 billion as demand for its high-end artificial intelligence chips continued to outstrip the company's ability to supply them. The results, released Wednesday, mark the latest evidence that spending on AI infrastructure by major technology companies remains robust even as some investors grow more cautious about how long the current pace of investment can be sustained.

Net income for the May-to-July period nearly tripled from $26.42 billion a year earlier, translating to earnings of $2.46 per share. Stripping out certain one-time items, adjusted earnings came in at $2.22 per share, comfortably ahead of the $2.09 per share analysts had projected, according to FactSet consensus estimates compiled ahead of the report. Revenue more than doubled year over year and topped the average Wall Street forecast of $92.27 billion.
Earnings and Revenue Growth Beat Wall Street Forecasts

Nvidia's net income figure included a $7.8 billion gain tied to the company's equity investments in other firms, including stakes in Intel and SpaceX, following a similar $15.9 billion gain in the prior quarter. Those investment gains added to an already strong operating performance driven by chip sales, underscoring how Nvidia has increasingly used its cash position to take equity stakes in strategically important partners across the technology and aerospace sectors.

"AI has reached its inflection point. It's doing useful work. Its tokens are productive and profitable. Now, compute is revenue," Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said in a statement accompanying the results. The comment reflects a shift in how Nvidia frames its business, from selling chips primarily for AI model training toward positioning its hardware as the backbone of AI systems that are now generating measurable economic output for customers.
Data Center Business Fuels the Bulk of Growth

Nvidia's data center segment, which includes AI-focused data center hardware and chip sales to hyperscale cloud operators such as Amazon, Microsoft, Google and Meta, generated $89 billion in revenue, more than double what it produced a year earlier and ahead of analyst expectations of roughly $86.33 billion. The segment now accounts for approximately 92% of Nvidia's total revenue, reflecting how thoroughly the company's business has become concentrated around AI infrastructure demand relative to its more traditional gaming and graphics chip roots.

Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress told analysts on the earnings call that capital spending among the top five hyperscale cloud providers is projected to reach nearly $800 billion this year and climb to roughly $1.3 trillion in 2027, underscoring the scale of AI infrastructure investment that continues to flow toward companies like Nvidia. On the day of the earnings release, Nvidia and Amazon Web Services separately announced plans to deploy 2 million additional Nvidia graphics processing units, along with an agreement to incorporate Nvidia chips into Amazon's fleet of warehouse robots.
Supply Constraints Are Limiting How Fast Nvidia Can Grow

Even with blockbuster results, Nvidia's leadership emphasized that the company's growth remains capped by how much product it can actually manufacture and ship. "Our entire supply chain is challenged," Huang told analysts. "At this point we have supply for 70%. ... Our demand is much higher than that." Kress echoed that point, noting that Nvidia's growth outlook for its next fiscal year would be closer to double the projected 70% rate if supply constraints weren't limiting how much of that demand the company can currently fulfill, based on forecasts shared by its own customers.

Operating expenses climbed alongside revenue, rising 55% year over year to $8.41 billion, reflecting the scale of investment Nvidia is making in research, staffing and supply chain commitments to keep pace with demand. The company also disclosed that its supply commitments, largely tied to memory procurement, more than doubled from $119 billion in the prior quarter to $279 billion in the most recent period, a sign of how aggressively Nvidia is locking in manufacturing capacity to support future growth.
Forward Guidance Points to Accelerating Growth

For the current quarter, Nvidia forecast revenue of approximately $108 billion, ahead of the $104.86 billion analysts had penciled in. Meeting that target would represent an increase of roughly 89% from the same period last year, suggesting Nvidia's growth rate is still accelerating rather than slowing as the AI infrastructure buildout matures. Notably, the company said its outlook assumes no data center compute revenue from China, reflecting the ongoing impact of export restrictions on that market.

Looking further ahead, Nvidia said it expects revenue for its fiscal year ending January 2028 to grow by approximately 70%, a figure that itself surprised some analysts who had been modeling slower growth deceleration heading into that period. Kress also said the company expects its central processing unit revenue to more than double in fiscal 2028, a shift the company said would position it as one of the world's leading server CPU suppliers alongside its dominant position in AI accelerators.
Capital Returns and Shareholder Payouts

Alongside its growth investments, Nvidia continued returning capital to shareholders, spending $26 billion on share repurchases and dividends during the quarter. The company previously told investors in May that it had authorized an additional $80 billion in buybacks, and it also announced plans to pay a 25-cent-per-share dividend, continuing a pattern of increased capital returns as both revenue and free cash flow have expanded rapidly in recent years.
How Markets and Investors Reacted

Nvidia shares initially closed the regular trading session down 1.6% on the day of the report, before climbing 4.1% in after-hours trading once the results and guidance were released. The stock is up 12.4% so far this year, a more modest gain relative to Nvidia's outsized rallies in prior years of the AI boom, reflecting a market that has grown somewhat more measured in how it prices in the company's continued outperformance.

The company's edge computing segment, which covers chips that bring AI capabilities to personal computers, gaming consoles and robotics, posted revenue of $7.2 billion, up 27% from the same period a year earlier. While a much smaller contributor than the data center business, the segment reflects Nvidia's continued push to extend AI processing capability beyond large cloud data centers and into a broader range of consumer and industrial devices.
Questions About AI Spending Sustainability Persist

Despite the strength of the results, a segment of investors and analysts remain cautious about the durability of the current AI investment cycle. Nvidia's market valuation has climbed from roughly $400 billion at the end of 2022 to approximately $5.2 trillion today, a rise that has made the company one of the most closely watched bellwethers for the broader technology sector and for AI-driven market gains more broadly.
